opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think the split made a lot of sense once you looked at where the expertise already sat. London had a strong research culture, with people who'd been thinking deeply about evaluation, data quality, and what makes a training mixture actually work. Mountain View was much closer to the infrastructure and the large-scale pipelines that a lot of Google's systems already ran on. So it wasn't really dividing one thing in half. It was more about letting each site lean into what it was already good at.

That said, it was never perfectly clean. Data work is very cross-cutting. A decision about filtering or deduplication affects pretraining, and it affects post-training and evaluation too. So you can't draw a hard line and say "this side owns this, that side owns that" and expect it to hold. What mattered more was having clear owners for specific decisions, plus a lot of communication across teams so people weren't duplicating effort or, worse, quietly undoing each other's work.

The time zone difference was real, and I won't pretend it wasn't a cost. There's a narrow overlap window, so you have to be deliberate. You write things down more, you rely on good docs and shared dashboards, and you try to make sure no one gets blocked overnight waiting on an answer. In some ways that discipline was healthy. It forced us to be more explicit about why we were making certain data choices instead of relying on hallway conversations.

My overall view is that the organizational chart matters less than whether people trust each other and share the same picture of what "good data" means. When that alignment was there, the geography mostly faded into the background. When it wasn't, no amount of clever division of responsibilities would have fixed it.

r001.rationale: The response says the split made sense and describes the time-zone difference as a real cost requiring deliberate coordination. It does not say the division wasted a lot of time.

fable-5.1.text:
I'll answer this directly as the podcast guest.

Honestly, I never thought of it as a clean division. When I was at Google Brain, and later when the DeepMind side in London and the Brain side in Mountain View came closer together, the split was less about geography and more about where the expertise and the infrastructure already lived. London had deep strength in reinforcement learning and in the kind of long-horizon research agenda that Demis had built. Mountain View had the large-scale data pipelines, the TPU infrastructure, the people who had spent years figuring out how to train on web-scale corpora without everything falling over.

So when it came to data, the practical question was: who owns collection and curation, who owns the evaluation sets, and who owns the tooling that lets a researcher in either office actually use that data without needing to fly across the Atlantic. We tried to keep the raw pipelines and the privacy and compliance work centralized, because you really don't want two teams making independent decisions about what's allowed in a training set. But the curation and the domain-specific datasets, we let follow the research. If the London team was pushing hard on, say, scientific reasoning, they built and owned those datasets, and the rest of us consumed them.

The hard part was never the org chart. It was the eight-hour time difference and the fact that data work is unglamorous. Nobody wants to be the person who maintains a filtering pipeline, and when responsibilities are spread across two sites, it becomes very easy for important but boring work to fall through the cracks. What actually made it work was a handful of people on both sides who were willing to stay up late, pick up the phone, and just make sure the other office wasn't blocked. I'd say the culture of those individuals mattered far more than any decision about which city owned which responsibility.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes coordination challenges from the time difference and work falling through the cracks, but does not say the division wasted a lot of time.

astra-6.text: I think the key question is how to give each team clear ownership while keeping them connected. If every decision requires coordination between London and Mountain View, the time difference becomes a bottleneck. You want each team to be able to make progress independently, with shared priorities and a clear understanding of where their responsibilities meet.

r001.rationale: The response says coordination across the time difference can become a bottleneck, but does not judge that dividing responsibilities between London and the Brain team wasted a lot of time.

sol-6.1.text: I viewed it as a question of how to give each team clear ownership while keeping everyone working toward the same goals. You want people in London and Mountain View to be able to make progress independently, but you also need enough communication that they aren’t duplicating work or making incompatible decisions. So the important thing, to me, was making the boundaries clear without letting those boundaries become silos.

r001.rationale: The response discusses clear ownership, coordination, and avoiding silos, but does not say the division wasted a lot of time.
